utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the president of the Presidency was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was Alija Izetbegovic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he became that because Fikret Abdic, who won more votes than he did, ceded his position to him though the prior agreement had been that the person who won most votes would become president.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in view of the customary principle of equality of all three nations, the president of the whole assembly consisting of both Muslims, Croats, and Serb, was a Serb, wasn't he, Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when the division occurred, then Momcilo Krajisnik remained president but only president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after the proclamation of independence, without the participation of the Serb people in that referendum, the Serb representatives from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina were virtually eliminated; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now when we look at the differences between Variant A and B, Variant A refers to those municipalities in which the Serbs have a majority, which means they have a majority in the municipal assembly and in which Serb representatives do have a hold on power. They are in power.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you then to read the second level of this Variant A, which has to do with municipalities with a Serb majority, and point 8 of this second level, that is, the municipalities in which Serbs are in power, Variant A I'm talking about, and it says: "In taking all these measures, attention should be paid to ensuring respect for the national and other rights of members of all nationalities and engage them later in government bodies which will be established by the Assembly of the Serb People in the municipality." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So where the Serbs are in power and where after the proclamation of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina they come into power, there is emphasis on the need to respect the rights of nations; whereas, in the municipalities where the Serbs are not in power, efforts were made in some way to rally together and protect the Serb part of the population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And there is only one other difference, where in the second level it says: "The branch offices of the SDK are obliged to prevent an outflow of cash and securities from the vaults under their control at banks, post offices, and other financial organisations, as well as to speed up the daily monitoring of the payment system in their own area." This is point 4. So the instruction is to prevent wasting of cash and withdrawal, outflows of cash and securities. So I haven't been able to identify any other difference between Variant A and B because everything else, like protecting people, children, pregnant women, the sick, the disabled, et cetera, these things apply to both Variant A and Variant B. So can we draw the conclusion that the key difference in Variant A, which refers to municipalities in which the Serbs are in power, is the emphasis that the government which is already in their hands must pay attention, and I quote, "To ensuring respect for the national and other rights of members of all nationalities and their late engagement in government bodies."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were in possession of these instructions for much longer than I was, you analysed it and implemented it, did you notice any other difference between Variant A and B?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view too, the only difference in Variant B is that the Serbs where they are in a minority, to try to rally and to try and link up with any larger Serb territories with a view to protecting the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true -- or rather, it is common knowledge, I would say, that Bosnia and Herzegovina was internationally recognised on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that that was when a soldier was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the killing of a soldier coincided with the recognition on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this was a symbolic date, because the 6th of April is the day when Hitler attacked Yugoslavia in 1941; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs did not recognise the independence of Bosnia, and then they formed a provisional government; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had our own referendum of the Serb people, at which we declared that we would not accept such an international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we did not take part in the referendum organised by the Muslims and Croats for independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us not go into constitution and legal matters now, because even though I do believe that you are familiar with these things, you are not an expert in that field. Was it the practice and was the legal situation in B and H throughout the period prior to this to show maximum respect for members of all three nations, or rather, for decisions to be taken by consensus of all three nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the practice. And in my personal opinion, that was the only solution had it remained as it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So by a referendum in which the Serbs did not participate, do you feel that the Serbs assessed that their rights had been infringed upon rightly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what we believed, and 99 per cent of the Serbs did not support that option.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now, at least when we are talking about a political approach on the part of all parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the International Community, isn't the main principle the equality of all three ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to our constitution and according to the government measures. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So with the outbreak of the war and after the end of -- prior to the outbreak of the war and after the end of the war, the equality of all three nations is respected and decisions need to be taken by consensus.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the principle applied today too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when the war broke out, that principle was not observed at the expense of the Serb people; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our assessment at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, independence was recognised; Bosnia was recognised, soldiers killed. And this happened on the 8th of April, what happened in Zvornik, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened in Zvornik, was it a consequence of these events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my testimony that a consequence of was the international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the killing of the soldier was pouring oil on the flames of the situation as it was already at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your oral testimony, according to my notes, that after the outbreak of the conflict in Zvornik volunteers started arriving from Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why is it -- just one moment. Let me see if I understand this. Why was it necessary for the Serbs to take Zvornik municipality? Why was that seen as a necessary action? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't considered a necessary action. I didn't see that there was any plan to take Zvornik municipality. In accordance with Plan B, we withdrew to territory in which the Serbs had a majority, that is, around Karakaj and down the Drina River. However, in Mali Zvornik, we tried twice to agree with the Bosniaks on some sort of a status quo and to see what the solution would be for the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but with the arrival of Arkan and the slapping around of members of the Crisis Staff, he started slapping us around and asked us, "Who gave you the authority to negotiate with them, to sell out Serb land? This is Serbian." And he ordered an attack on Zvornik to be prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you effectively blame the paramilitaries and Arkan in particular for what happened in the municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying here and claiming that while I was a member of the Crisis Staff we never mentioned the possibility of attacking Zvornik militarily because the Muslim population accounted for about 75 or 76 per cent of the population according to the 1991 census, but we were all beaten, we were all lined up, and we were ordered. Actually, other men took over control over the staff. At least, that was my understanding, and that is why I left it. We were no longer in control. We had to stand at attention when Arkan walked in or his deputy Pejic and we were in a subordinate position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you brought Arkan to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't bring him. I physically got in touch with him. I was the first one to get in touch with him from the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that was in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as you yourself said, you brought him to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. His unit with Pejic was accommodated in Radanj and then he came to Zvornik later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he came later. But you brought the unit with Pejic at its head and put them up in Radanj; is that right? And at the time, you were a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Crisis Staff at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were chief of police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Well, that is more or less the same thing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. It's a big difference, Mr. Milosevic. Chief of police is one thing, and commander of the police station is another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Explain to me now, please, why on the basis of what you said - and I took note of it somewhere - that they said, "In the event of an outbreak of conflict, they were there to assist the Serb people." This was said by Arkan or Pejic; I'm not sure which. I took note of it here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pejic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. The person you met. So he represented that unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he said that should a conflict occur, they were there to assist the Serb people in Zvornik. That is what he said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then how do you then explain that they provoked the attack on Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you this. You can invite somebody to your house as a guest and they take -- abuse your hospitality and take over control and command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see from my notes, as Mr. Groome put a question to you as to how long Arkan was in Zvornik, and you said he was there twice for one or two hours each time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then later on, when he left, then others took over command. What command could he have had over Zvornik if he was there twice for an hour or two each time? And I quoted you as saying that this one, this Pejic said that they were there to assist the Serb people should a conflict arise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must be some confusion. When I said that Arkan was in command, I meant while his unit was there. I'm testifying that throughout the stay -- his stay in Zvornik, whether it was he or Pejic, but his unit, while they were in Zvornik no one had any say about anything from little things to big things in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Only 20 men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had 20-odd men. But the problem is that at the beginning, all those volunteer units who had spent time at various theatres of war all over Croatia and elsewhere placed themselves under his control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that the volunteers started coming in after the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that a group of volunteers started coming in, starting on the 6th of April, immediately when the incidents broke out and when we went out to Karakaj. But most arrived a day before the attack and on the actual day of the attack on Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But when you were asked about the number, you said -- I wrote this down -- that "There were over 100 volunteers from Serbia." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were certainly more than 100 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So about 100 volunteers from Serbia. And what about the Territorial Defence of Zvornik? How many people were there then and the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had about 30 to 40 Serb policemen who were there at the police station. We had about 200 men from the Territorial Defence. Because the rest were deployed in their own villages, and they had also been surrounded. However, you have to know that at that time we did not know what a war was and what kind of an experience this was; whereas, almost 90 per cent of those people had already had the experience of war from Croatia and they knew about all these variants and about the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. psychological effects of warfare and so on and so forth, whereas we were taken aback at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted to clarify these facts. So about 100 volunteers came to help you, and then it turned out that these volunteers who had come to help you to defend yourselves, and as you said yourself in case a conflict broke out to help the Serb people, that they actually caused the conflict, and that without their presence this conflict never would have occurred. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that the Crisis Staff tried all the time to work out an agreement with the SDA, that it was politically in charge of Zvornik and had Zvornik under its control. And I never attended a meeting of the Crisis Staff where people said that Zvornik should be attacked or taken over militarily. And I claim that when Arkan came, the Crisis Staff was beaten up, slapped around. He talked about it publicly several times, about ten times on TV, in the media, and he said that Zvornik had to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He beat you up? He slapped you around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, me inter alia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Arkan is the one who caused the war in Zvornik? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not trying to say that without Arkan there wouldn't have been a war in Zvornik. I'm saying that the direct order issuing authority for the attack on Zvornik was him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that there would not have been a war in Zvornik without him? What you did, at the level of Zvornik, when you were endeavouring to work out a solution with the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the same thing that the leadership did within Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serb side, were they trying to work out a solution with the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I testified here about the things I know and the things I saw, and this is a hypothetical question. What would have happened if the order to attack Zvornik had not been issued?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're asked a question you can't give the answer to, just say so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you followed these instructions that we commented upon a while ago. You establish a Territorial Defence. You distribute weapons to Serb villages depending on their degree of endangerment. And you establish the Serb authorities. You have the Serb police, and so on and so forth. And all of this is beyond all these events that occurred. And then about 20 men come in, 20 men that you brought in from Bijeljina, 20 of Arkan's men, and then they're the ones who caused the conflict in Zvornik. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, according to Variant B, we did what had been envisaged. We withdrew to the territory where the Serbs had a majority. We separated our government authorities, and this Variant B, there is no mention of us taking over towns where the Muslims were a majority. So I am saying what I know because I was present there. In the Crisis Staff we never had any discussions about taking over Zvornik militarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you do claim that Arkan with 20 men would have taken it over. You said a while ago that there were 500 reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think he's given his answers about this. And there's a limit to what he can be asked.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wrote this down here, that you said the first morning at the staff you were in slippers, you said, because you had been wounded. The TO units and the volunteers took over Zvornik and put it under Serb control. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days before that, at the staff, a member of the Crisis Staff dropped the detonator from a hand grenade and just this one little part and that's how I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was the provisional government established in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when this happened, but after the Crisis Staff they appeared as the highest-ranking civilian authority. So it was the provisional government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: You said -- actually, we clarified a while ago that in this conflict in Zvornik the JNA did not participate at all. But then later on you talk about Captain Obrenovic from the JNA. And in these tabs we saw that he was receiving a salary as a member of the Territorial Defence of the Municipal Assembly of Zvornik. So is this a representative of the Army of Republika Srpska who had been a member of the JNA before, or are we talking about a JNA unit that was present there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obrenovic changed various ranks, from captain to lieutenant colonel. He came to the area of Zvornik as a JNA unit before the conflict broke out, perhaps a few months prior to that. He was there throughout. And I know because he comes from Rogatica, which is in Republika Srpska. When the Army of Republika Srpska was established, he transferred into the regular Army of Republika Srpska. I know that he received a salary from the JNA and also from the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify this, then. Captain Obrenovic is a man from Republika Srpska who, as you say, a few months before that had been in the JNA while the JNA was in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a regular army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Later on, when the JNA withdrew, a number of officers, soldiers stayed behind, those who originally came from Republika Srpska, the Army of Republika Srpska was established and he was an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And towards the end of May 1992, you say the Zvornik Brigade was established of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the commanders changed, and only towards the end of 1992 this command was stabilised; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And why was this Marko Pavlovic arrested, who was commander of the TO? I wrote this down here. You said he was arrested by the special unit of the police of Republika Srpska in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was arrested in this particular operation, when quite a few volunteers were captured. I don't know why he was arrested, but I know that he did spend some time in detention in Bijeljina, and after that I read in the papers that he had been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for the presence of volunteers, in the questions that were put to you here a unit of the Territorial Defence from Loznica is mentioned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know which segment you're looking at right now, but I don't really find this very clear. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were volunteers from Loznica, but this was not a TO unit from Loznica. These were volunteers from Loznica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is beyond any dispute. There was no unit from Loznica. There were volunteers from Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is what I wanted us to clarify in order to prevent any kind of manipulation. Again, you talk about Karisik. Karisik was chief of the military police or chief of police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was head of the special police of the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now I have information here that their task was to arrest members of various paramilitary units that were disturbing the peace in town or that were involved in any kind of crime.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from the top echelons of Republika Srpska this unit had to be commanded or at least it had to be the top of the Ministry of the Interior that had to issue orders to them. Their task was to arrest those who were creating unrest in town or committing crimes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they actually doing this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think this is well known that towards the end of July they did arrest about 20 people in Zvornik, including Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was stressed several times here that Biljana Plavsic came there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said before and after the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: She came in her capacity as member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina or vice-president of the presidency of Republika Srpska, was that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no Republika Srpska presidency at the time. She was then a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The only reason why she came there was to familiarise herself with the situation there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the area, at local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: She tried to work in favour of calming the situation down; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation did not calm down. The leadership of Republika Srpska and we at local level had already started carrying out this plan, and we did not recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina as it was recognised internationally and under the conditions under which it had been recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know who invited this unit, Arkan's unit, the Serb Volunteer Guard? Who asked them to come to Bijeljina. From Bijeljina they came to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The first time I heard of Arkan's unit was when the Oslobodjenje daily newspaper wrote about it. I remember that on the front page there was a photograph from Bijeljina and a headline saying "Arkan killing and looting," something to that effect. But I don't know who brought him to Bijeljina, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he killing and looting though?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what happened in Bijeljina. I was in Bijeljina only for an hour, and I was on the premises of the cultural centre, so I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about what happened in Bijeljina and about the way they came there? You only know about their number and how they actually arrived in Hotel Radanj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything I know about Bijeljina is what I read about in the newspapers or what I heard about from other people, but I personally do not have any knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that later your company had and put at the disposal of the Army of Republika Srpska, as you had put it yourself, two or three trucks. Your company was engaged for these priority needs of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a state-owned company, a socially-owned company, where I was general manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what these trucks transported?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went on these trucks, and I don't know what they transported. I only heard the comments of the drivers. They said that they were transporting things that were required by the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it food, blankets, wheat, flour, sugar, oil, other things that were coming in by way of assistance, aid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is indirect. I'm saying what I heard about from others. But they were transporting food, footwear, clothing, and military equipment, anything they were ordered to transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that this was regular procedure. Civilian trucks and also customs procedure was followed. It wasn't that customs duty was paid, but customs recorded all of this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for tax purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of these customs records, do you know about what kind of goods were involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, as the actual forwarders, did not get this from the customs offices. This was done for the purposes of the TO. So we only got the commercial documents involved. However, from the moment when the truck was engaged until it returned, I as general manager and my co-workers did not have any control over these vehicles, nor did we have any insight into what they were actually transporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. B-024: When did you become a member of the Serb Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I became a member of the Serb Democratic Party in 1991, sometime in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you voluntarily joined the SDS.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the reason for your joining this party? There were other parties too, in addition to the SDA. I understand that you would not have joined the SDA, and I imagine there was no HDZ in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was a negligible number of Croats in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So what was the reason for your decision to join this political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, national parties were established in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this led to a total polarisation among the people. And in fact, 95 per cent of the Serbs joined the SDA -- no, I'm sorry, the SDS and 95 per cent of the Muslims to the SDA and the Croats had an even larger percentage in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I imagine that when you acceded to this political party you actually agreed with its objectives and those of its president, Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but then Radovan Karadzic at that time was an unknown person. The key point was for us to remain together with Serbia. This part of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina had as the key programme of the party not to allow Yugoslavia to break up, and we wanted to go on living together with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now: Since you were shown various payrolls here - I don't want to waste any time in this respect. You were already given all of this, these different tabs - payrolls of members of the TO of Zvornik. You remember that? We don't have to get them out; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These were in fact people who were employed in the Zvornik municipality, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were those employees and the Territorial Defence and the police were also given their salaries from there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the question. The interpreters apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They received it from the budget of the provisional government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, how did the provisional leadership come by the funds and money they needed for their budget for paying out the salaries and all the other expenditure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were two ways in which this was done. The municipality had its regular incomes and revenues. I don't want to go into the details of where this came from. And the other way is that there were taxes that the municipality imposed on companies, and they would have to pay a certain amount of money to -- for the budget from its incomes and revenues in order to finance this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And if one were to add up all this, these were the usual -- this was the usual way in which this was done, through taxation and so on, the moneys accrued in this way and which were customary in peacetime as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody from the territory of your municipality, somebody who was a member of the municipal organs, bodies, Territorial Defence, or anything of that kind, were they paid by a state organ from the Republic of Serbia at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge. As far as I know, nobody was paid from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your microphone isn't on. Yes. Start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true, apart from these taxes, the taxation that you mentioned, many economic legal entities from the Zvornik area, did they contribute besides what they were legally bound to do, in view of the general, social needs and circumstances in those times of crisis in Zvornik? Did they contribute at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. And the whole of the economy, we could say, served the function of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All of them, to all intents and purposes; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 13 of the transcript, you said that the various Zvornik enterprises, Metalka, et cetera, helped out. You only quoted that by way of an example, because all the economic enterprises helped.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right. There were no exceptions. Each gave as much as they were able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let's put that right then. I understood you to say that the money was used to finance some wartime expenditures of the municipality. It wasn't wartime expenditures. It was the overall expenditures of the municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely correct. For all expenditures, overall expenditures. Of course, during the war, the war expenditure amounted to the highest amounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't you say that the highest amount was paid out by way of salaries for the territorials?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you consider, since you had an insight into what was going on, that the money that was collected by the municipality was used for set purposes, pursuant to the law and rules and regulations and the decisions that you yourselves made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different controls that were -- and checks that were conducted, and it was never abused. The local authorities, of course, would pinpoint the priority areas to be financed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the municipality paid from those funds various volunteer units too, or rather, volunteers, regardless whether they were units or not, but let's say volunteers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the volunteers were very welcome, because we were in the minority, so it was our position that we should treat volunteers just like any other regular soldier in the TO, that they be given equal treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to clear one point up: In your statement - I think it was on page 9; yes, it was - you said that the official policy of Serbia stood behind Arkan. Where did you get that from? How come you get that idea, and did you really say what it says in the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I also added that that was my personal impression, in view of the fact that he came to Zvornik for the first time wearing -- or rather, in a police vehicle. He came officially, passing through official checkpoints, across the bridge. So that's the impression I gained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was just your personal impression. And if I recall correctly, I think you said that the police vehicle had the license plates denoting the federal SUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I worked in the police force, I could distinguish between the license plates and numbers. We had different numbers for each individual republic. And the Federal SUP would have 9 as the initial digit. And he arrived in a Golf which belonged to the Federal SUP, and the license Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. plates began with the number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And apart from the fact that this was your impression, gained on the basis of the license plates of the Federal SUP on the Golf vehicle, Volkswagen Golf vehicle, which brought Arkan to Zvornik, were you able to gain this impression from anything else, in any other way, by any kind of support on the part of the representative of any state organ of Serbia, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that during my testimony, that apart from the fact that there was a lot of media coverage by certain papers, I have no official knowledge about his contacts with certain individuals, and I know that Kostic always spoke in negative terms about him and his human side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the man you've just mentioned I believe was in the organs of Serbia. Was he a member of Serb organs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that he was an employee of that institution, but my contacts with him were of a private nature. I would never go to see him in his office. We would either meet at my home or his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In view of the position that you held, do you happen to recall that it was precisely the leadership of the republic of Serbia which categorically strove to ensure that any kind of unit or volunteers had to be placed under the command of the JNA and that was the only armed force that we considered to be the legal and legitimate armed force? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one were to watch television at the time and read the paper, then one would know that that was the official position taken by the authorities in Serbia. I was one of the people that did watch television and read the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And let me add to this. I'm sure you'll remember that the JNA was accused for the fact that -- of the support it enjoyed by the leadership of Serbia as an integrative part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but bear in mind that I'm talk about the situation in the field, on the ground. I know what the official policy was. But of course when it was translated into practice, things didn't always follow that pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me this: What were your assignments and duties in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of the police station. That was my task. Because all these were delineated in the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff came into being following on from Variant A and B, and it stipulated which officials would be part of the Crisis Staff. As the commander of the police station, I became a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Brano Grujic was the president at that time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brano Grujic was the president of the Crisis Staff, yes, at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that he can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asked to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked whether you were on good terms with Mr. Grujic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that he performed his duties in a proper and correct manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, while I was in the Crisis Staff, yes, I do think his conduct was proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Did you consider that the establishment of the Crisis Staff was indispensable in view of the overall situation in those areas, in the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of us in Zvornik agreed that it was absolutely necessary to establish a Crisis Staff, and not only in Zvornik. It was established in all the municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 7, points 4 to 9, under number 6 you state that it was the general position taken -- official position taken by the leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and with you too that on the territory which was under Serb control the Muslims must be accepted as being citizens of equality -- on a footing of equality like the Serb population. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in that statement, under point A, I mention Plan A and Plan B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, but very briefly: What was your attitude and position towards the disruption -- to the disruption of Yugoslavia or the disintegration of Yugoslavia? Because I don't want it to be a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this? You've asked him -- you've asked him about what was happening in the municipality. You've asked him about his political views. What is the relevance of his attitude towards the disruption of Yugoslavia? He said, as I understood it, that he wanted all the Serbs -- wanted to live with the Serbs in Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about Yugoslavia, Mr. May, not about Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, what is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I say "you," when I use the V, the second person plural, I'm not thinking about him personally. I'm referring to the population of that region. And I'm asking you -- I'm asking him whether it is clear that the -- practically the entire population was in favour of preserving Yugoslavia over there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is unequivocally correct, without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's clarify that. The entire population or the entire Serb population?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Serb population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that quite a lot of the Muslim inhabitants were also in favour of preserving Yugoslavia? Would that be true too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that a portion of the Muslims, a smaller portion, were in favour of preserving Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this break-up or disintegration came from the leadership, not the people, when we're talking about the Muslims; is that right? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think that's a matter for this witness. It may be a matter we'll have to decide in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me now in general terms, but briefly, please: Did the Serbs in Zvornik prepare themselves for a defence or for an aggression of some kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said this on a number of occasions here, exclusively for defence purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please - and I just have a few questions related to something that you spoke about this morning in part - on page 52, in fact, of this statement of yours you say that Grujic told you that General Subotic had come to Zvornik with the task of destroying mass graves. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell me first, who is General Subotic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know him personally. I met him at Grujic's house. He's a man I know who for a time performed the function of the Minister of Defence in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Minister or deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the Minister of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please: Was anybody else present when Grujic told you this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You don't talk about things like that in a large company.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did these mass graves exist at all, the mass graves that Subotic was supposed to remove or liquidate, judging by what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the knowledge I have so far and the information media, quite obviously some did exist. Some have been. Some were uncovered and proved to have existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about the information media. I'm asking about you personally. You were in Zvornik throughout, and you say that Grujic told you that Subotic had arrived to destroy this. A moment ago we noted that you would have had to have known what they knew. So did these mass graves exist in Zvornik or did they not? Did you know about these mass graves or did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, up until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer in his own way. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was there until the 20th of April, in the Crisis Staff, that is. And I can say with full responsibility that no mass graves existed until that time. After that, I didn't work in the police. I wasn't a member of the Crisis Staff after that. And I can only say what was rumoured and the stories that were told. I have no personal knowledge about the existence of these mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge at all about the fact that they existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I have an awareness of this from the information media and from what was generally known, but I personally do not have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you personally, because you're testifying here now. Now, what the information media say, anybody can read that. You were asked by Mr. Groome who you recognised from the tape. You said that it was played extensively on television programmes dating back to 1997, the celebration. That's what I'm talking about, the specials operations units in Kula. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you recognised Lukovic, Legija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you also said that you recognised Captain Dragan; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these were the two men that you recognised.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, is it true that when it comes to Lukovic, Legija, because he asked you about who you recognised in Zvornik, that at the time he was a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guards of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He had nothing to do with the police of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. In 1992, I do know that he had no links with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And with respect to Captain Dragan, we noted that he didn't have a unit of any kind over there but came with two or three men who were instructors to assist in the training of the territorial men, engaged in Territorial Defence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, explain this to me, please, what you were asked by

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He asked you about the attack on Divic. Is it true that the JNA did not take part in the attack on Divic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did any unit from Serbia take part in the attack on Divic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which unit. But I do know that from Mali Zvornik and this part of Serbia, from the side of Serbia fire was opened towards Divic. And there is still evidence of bullet shots. But which were the units opening fire, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said somebody from the hydro powerplant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that's what you mean when you say from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the hydro powerplant is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. But it's on the Drina, isn't it? The dam, as far as I know, is between two banks of the river, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When talking very briefly about this event in Celopek, without going into all the details of those events, is it true that the perpetrators were arrested not only by the police in Yugoslavia but in cooperation with the police of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is generally known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the police from Serbia and the police of Republika Srpska arrested that group together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wish to underline this, because you must have known this, first of all. And secondly, it is being attributed to the police of Republika Srpska, but the police of Republika Srpska took part in their arrest and not in the event, to make this quite clear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, this event in connection with Karakaj, it's not clear to me. According to information I have, the people who were detained there were driven off for some sort of an exchange from there. Even a witness a few days ago, speaking about the detainees held in Pilica - is the name in the nominative Pilice or Pilica - that they were driven off for an exchange afterwards. Can you tell me anything about what actually happened there, as far as you know, according to your own knowledge, aside from the rumours? Do you have any personal knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This morning, answering a similar question, I said that the people had surrendered. The men were separated from the women and children. The women and children were sent to Kalesija. The men were rounded up in the school in Karakaj. Two men were driven off to be exchanged. And they took with them a list to Tuzla, to hand in to the staff in Tuzla, to try and exchange. And I know that those two men, Aga Lupic is one name, and another one, Alijic, the president of the SDA. They left and took this list of people who were left behind at the school in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, two men from this group were sent to Tuzla to the authorities under Muslim control; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To take with them a list and propose an exchange for the detained Serbs held by the Muslim authorities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, explain to me, please: Do you know anything about those people being killed? I don't mean those two men who went to Tuzla with the list, but these others who were left behind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no direct knowledge. I know that the people were in custody at the school in Karakaj. What happened later on, I don't know. But only what everyone knows from the press, that the people were killed and that some were found in mass graves as bodies -- or rather, dead bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you have no personal knowledge. All the personal knowledge you have is what you already told me in answer to one of my questions, when you said that Karakaj was under the control of the Zvornik police and the Territorial Defence of Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you make inquiries later on, among them to learn whether those people had been exchanged, how many had been killed, how many had been exchanged, and so on? Do you have any idea about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I personally do not know what happened. But the original story was that they were taken to be exchanged at Batkovic. After that -- very shortly after that, there was rumours in Zvornik that those people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I want to make it quite clear. You referred to Kozluk. Was anyone killed in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information that anyone was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who ordered the people to leave Kozluk? I assume that you know that a list of citizens of Kozluk was sent, that is, people who wanted to move out, and that they moved out through Serbia and those who entered Serbia, left Serbia and went to third places. Did anyone force them? Did they leave because of the danger that threatened them? Who organised it? Who ordered it? Did anyone force them out by force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in July. I was not a member of the Crisis Staff by then, and I really don't know the details. I know that in April we persuaded them not to move out of Kozluk. We provided some basic requirements that they needed, like healthcare, food, et cetera. As to what happened later on, I know as much as everyone else from stories that went round town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wonder if you could try and assist me in clearing up another question that you mentioned this morning. That was mentioned only in passing. Mr. Groome was asking you something in connection with the report of the Drinatrans about a transport. And then you say Zvornik-Bijeljina-Batkovic on the 15th of July 600 detainees. And from the information I have, this Batkovic was a centre for exchange and the Red Cross was continuously present there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went to Batkovic, but I heard the same report as you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the people who went to Batkovic, were they going to be exchanged or did perhaps somebody liquidate those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, except that I was able to reach the -- read the invoice, and one can see the figures. But I don't know what lies behind that invoice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all you know about Batkovic is what I mentioned just now, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let us look at a few other exhibits that I would like to ask you to clarify. For instance, this one, 13. Here the Basic Investment Bank in Belgrade, InvestBanka and then it says request for financial funds for the payment of April salaries, et cetera. This is the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik which sent this request?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- To pensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What it says here: "Basic economic investment bank in Belgrade has nothing to do with Belgrade because it is the business outlet in Tuzla." That's right. So it's a bank in Tuzla which was part of the system of a Yugoslav bank which had business branches all over Yugoslavia, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Branch offices all over Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, that bank covered the region of Tuzla and it was through it that pensions were paid.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this was a local institution, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just see a few other documents. I think this is tab 6, a list for payments of members of the TO of the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik for the month of May 1992. Again -- but I think we've cleared that up, and we know now that this was your own local institution making payments. I had a few other notes, but I must admit I don't find my way easily in these tabs. I wanted to ask you to explain, because this question refers to a period while you were still in office. What is this order? It is under tab -- I'll tell you in a minute -- number 9. It's an order on determining places for funerals and methods of burying persons killed in the war in the town of Zvornik and its environs, that is, within the territory of Zvornik municipality. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got that, Witness? You have it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then it says, under point 1, that "Muslims should be buried at the Muslim cemetery in Kazambasca." That was a Muslim cemetery, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Except for those whose bodies families take over in due time and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who wish to bury them somewhere else"; isn't that right? And then in point 2, at the Serb cemetery in Karakaj, "The killed should be buried that are known to be Serbs." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Except for those whose bodies are taken over by their families in due time who wish to bury them somewhere else." And then it also says that a commission should examine, identify, record, and select the various bodies, and this is an order which I assume -- it says "The provisional government of the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't -- we don't, in fact, have this document, do we? Unless it's part of something --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the right-hand side of the B/C/S version we have. We've had translated the left-hand side of the page, if you turn over the page in tab 9, go to the B/C/S version, it's the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we only translated the left-hand side, because that was the portion we intended to rely on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now that Mr. Milosevic has raised it, I've asked Ms. Wee to get a translation of the other side of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, without a doubt. Now, you've got five minutes left, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. I just wanted to clear this point up as well, Mr. May. Regardless of the fact that I see that it hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The date here is the 21st of April, which means two weeks -- almost two weeks after the outbreak of the conflict. So when some sort of order was being restored in Zvornik. So my question to you, Mr. B-024, is: This decision of the provisional government, does it testify to a non-discriminatory attitude, or rather completely equal-handed attitude towards people killed in the conflict, both Serbs and Muslims, during the conflict starting on the 8th of April? And in view of the position that you held at the time, could you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order published in the Official Gazette of Zvornik Municipality, and it is generally known. It came into effect the day after I left the Crisis Staff, which I left on the 12th of April. But it is obvious that it is as you say, an attempt to restore some sort of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me also, please: Apart from what you said, you were chief of police, did you have any other positions in Zvornik during this time, that is, from the beginning of 1992 onwards, until the end of the war that you're testifying about, the end being 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, from April, until the beginning of 1993, I was manager of Autotransport. Then I was president of the executive board of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were you president of the government, local government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the end of February until the beginning of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So virtually you were the town mayor of Zvornik in 1993/1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Only in 1993. From February 1993 until September. It is really the second by significance in the civilian authorities; the first being the president of the assembly, and the second being the president of the executive council or board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were the main figure of the executive branch of the authorities of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in those days, how were members of other ethnic groups treated, primarily Muslims in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was such, Mr. Milosevic, in 1993 that there were no Muslims in Zvornik, only those who might have been detained.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. We didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could count on the figures of one hand some mixed marriages. Because in our town there was total ethnic separation between May and June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did the Muslims from Zvornik go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly towards Tuzla and the internal part of the Federation; whereas, many refugees came from Tuzla and Zenica. There was a complete change of ethnic structure, a major migration of the population. So.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So refugees were coming from, where did you say, Zenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tuzla and the whole region.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. I'm sorry, we can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You'll have to get your microphone on. Make sure it's on. Yes, I know there's a difficulty with it. Just make sure the microphone is on. Have a pause between question and answer. Now, you've got -- you've got two minutes left for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. B-024: How many Serbs from Central Bosnia and the Tuzla region settled in Zvornik in those days and in 1993 when you headed the executive branch? I assume you had a clear idea about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 10 and 15 thousand people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 15 thousand people? And why did they come there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they had no conditions to live in Central Bosnia and because of fear of the war and the war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For the same reason for which Muslims had left Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any difference regarding those reasons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't see them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. May. That completes my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay. Do you have some questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's time for adjournment. It may be convenient afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's actually only one matter. It won't take very long at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It'll just package the witness in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness, if I can ask you about the pre-conflict time in Zvornik. I'm looking at a statement of yours, and you describe in that statement as the situation being very tense and the city was divided into ethnic groups. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that because people were aware generally of the issue that Bosnia may be declared an independent state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly because of that reason, and also because of the very bad experiences from previous wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In this statement as well, you describe in fact four or five soldiers being killed in a place called Sapna, within Zvornik municipality, on the day of the declaration of statehood. Is that right, the number, four or five soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the same information that I have, four to five soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And which soldiers were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were soldiers of the then-regular Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, can you deal with this in a few moments, or do you want longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have about a dozen questions. Perhaps after the break, if that's convenient for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, so the record is clear, during the cross-examination and I believe the examination by the amici, a document referred to as a statement -- has been referred to. In case of this witness, there has been no formal statement. What has been referred to is an interview conducted pursuant to Rule 42 and 43; a copy of it was disclosed. So it's a videotaped and transcribed interview. Your Honour, if I may, there was, I believe, a mistake in the transcript from the 23rd of May regarding the spelling of a name, although technically not part of re-examination. I'd seek leave just to ask the witness to spell the name so that can be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-024, on the first day you testified, you were asked a question regarding who headed the special police unit that arrested Marko Pavlovic and others. And you told us the first name of the question was Milenko. Can I ask you to repeat the last name, the family name of that person. Were you unable to hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's probably -- yes, I can hear you, yes. It's probably Milenko Mijic, who was chief of police at the beginning of the war in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to spell his name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: M-i-j-i-c, says the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] M-i-j-i-c, Mijic. Milenko is spelled, M-i-l-e-n-k-o.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at the end of the cross-examination, Mr. Milosevic has asked you about the period of time during which Muslims had control of the town. And you have referred to that period of time as several days. Can I ask you to describe as -- with as much precision as you can that period of time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can only be from the 5th of April, 1992 until the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I believe you said during that brief period of time that they assumed police functions and they also -- that there were no arrests during that period of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, on the 6th of April, the police of Zvornik split in two. I believe you testified earlier that the Serb portion of the police separated and started a parallel police department elsewhere in Zvornik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in accordance with Plan B we established a police station in the territory where there was a Serb majority population and that was in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during this three-day period when Muslims controlled the town of Zvornik, were there any summary executions of Serbs or any Serbs forcibly deported from the municipality of Zvornik, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I believe you testified in response to a question that Mr. Milosevic put to you that the takeover of Zvornik, the retaking of Zvornik or placing it in Serb control, took approximately four hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I meant that the military operation took from morning -- from the early morning hours, from 4.00 a.m., until 8.00 a.m. That is my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you testified in response to a question by Mr. Milosevic that paramilitaries slapped around members of the Crisis Staff. My question to you is: Were these local paramilitaries or were these the paramilitaries that you referred to as being from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said. It was Arkan and Pejic, people who were from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the destruction of mosques, how many mosques all together were destroyed in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
